learning_exercise.s2_body: Tap an option (or several if checkboxes appear) and use the yellow Send button below to submit. After sending, colours show correct, incorrect, or ruled-out choices.

practice_remix.s5_body: The list groups topics under class headings—scroll through the sections to mix areas from another grade or track.

practice_vs_machine.s3_body: Each row starts an AI duel with 10, 20, or 30 questions. Your score summary appears when the round ends.

profile_notifications.s3_body: Flip the toggle to opt in or out of OneSignal pushes. Status text beneath reflects the live subscription state.

profile_security.s3_body: Enter and confirm a new password, then hit Save. Visibility icons help you verify typing on small keyboards.

profile_about.s3_body: Open legal info, licences, release notes, or store reviews from these rows.
profile_about.s4_body: Use “Show tips” for the full tip list. Admins also see “Reset all screen tips” on this About screen to replay every guided tour from scratch.

profile_share.s3_body: Add up to four guardian addresses so reports can be shared responsibly. Saved entries show first; empty fields accept new mail.

profile_sound.s3_body: Toggle effects for feedback sounds and drag the slider to set loudness. A short sample plays when sound returns from silence.

not-found.title: 404 Not Found
not-found.text: Unfortunately we couldn't find the page you are looking for, but we find some information about famous mathematician. Enjoy :).
not-found.text-offline: You don't have internet, but we find some information about famous mathematician. Enjoy :).

mathematics.name: Pythagoras
mathematics.bio: Vegetarian mystical leader and number-obsessive, he owes his standing as the most famous name in maths due to a theorem about right-angled triangles, although it now appears it probably predated him. He lived in a community where numbers were venerated as much for their spiritual qualities as for their mathematical ones. His elevation of numbers as the essence of the world made him the towering primogenitor of Greek mathematics, essentially the beginning of mathematics as we know it now. And, famously, he didn't eat beans.

mathematics.name: Euclid
mathematics.bio: Known as the 'Father of Geometry', Euclid was an ancient Greek mathematician who wrote 'The Elements', one of the most influential works in the history of mathematics, which served as a main textbook for teaching mathematics until the late 19th century.

mathematics.name: Archimedes
mathematics.bio: Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287 – c. 212 BC) was an Ancient Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer, and inventor from the ancient city of Syracuse in Sicily. He is generally considered to be the greatest mathematician of antiquity and one of the greatest of all time, and gave the first satisfactory explanation of the principle of the lever. He is also credited with designing innovative machines, such as his screw pump, compound pulleys, and defensive war machines to protect his native Syracuse from invasion.

mathematics.name: Isaac Newton
mathematics.bio: Isaac Newton is one of the most famous scientists of all time, and he discovered some amazing things. He was the first to realize that white light is made up of all the colors of the rainbow. He invented calculus, the mathematics of moving things, which is used today to help us build skyscrapers and send rockets into space. He also figured out the force that pulls things to the ground – gravity. He was a strange character, who suffered from depression and rarely talked to anyone. He was also a secret alchemist, trying to turn lead into gold.

mathematics.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
mathematics.bio: Known as the prince of mathematicians, Gauss made significant contributions to most fields of 19th century mathematics. An obsessive perfectionist, he didn't publish much of his work, preferring to rework and improve theorems first. His revolutionary discovery of non-Euclidean space (that it is mathematically consistent that parallel lines may diverge) was found in his notes after his death. During his analysis of astronomical data, he realised that measurement error produced a bell curve – and that shape is now known as a Gaussian distribution.

mathematics.name: Leonhard Euler
mathematics.bio: The most prolific mathematician of all time, publishing close to 900 books. When he went blind in his late 50s his productivity in many areas increased. His famous formula `eiπ + 1 = 0`, where `e` is the mathematical constant sometimes known as Euler's number and `i` is the square root of minus one, is widely considered the most beautiful in mathematics. He later took an interest in Latin squares – grids where each row and column contains each member of a set of numbers or objects once. Without this work, we might not have had sudoku.

mathematics.name: René Descartes
mathematics.bio: Often referred to as the 'Father of Modern Philosophy', Descartes was also a key figure in mathematics for laying the foundation for the development of calculus and for his work in analytic geometry.

mathematics.name: Blaise Pascal
mathematics.bio: Mathematician and physicist Blaise Pascal is noted for his work in the fields of probability and fluid mechanics. His inventions include the Pascaline, an early calculator, and his contributions to hydrodynamics and pressure measurement.

mathematics.name: Pierre-Simon Laplace
mathematics.bio: Laplace was a mathematician and astronomer whose work was pivotal to the development of mathematical statistics, celestial mechanics, and the theory of probability.

mathematics.name: Bernhard Riemann
mathematics.bio: Known for the Riemann Hypothesis, one of the unsolved problems in mathematics, Riemann was a key figure in analysis and differential geometry, influencing areas such as number theory.

mathematics.name: Johannes Kepler
mathematics.bio: Kepler is best known for his laws of planetary motion, which laid the groundwork for Newton's theory of universal gravitation. His contributions to astronomy made him a key figure in the 17th-century scientific revolution.

mathematics.name: Évariste Galois
mathematics.bio: Galois was a pioneering figure in the development of abstract algebra. His work laid the foundations for group theory and was fundamental to the understanding of quadratic equations.

mathematics.name: David Hilbert
mathematics.bio: Hilbert was a leading figure in formalizing mathematics and developing mathematical logic. His 23 unsolved problems, presented at the International Congress of Mathematicians in 1900, set the agenda for much of 20th-century mathematics research.

mathematics.name: Georg Cantor
mathematics.bio: Of all the great mathematicians, Cantor most perfectly fulfils the (Hollywood) stereotype that a genius for maths and mental illness are somehow inextricable. Cantor's most brilliant insight was to develop a way to talk about mathematical infinity. His set theory led to the counter-intuitive discovery that some infinities were larger than others. The result was mind-blowing. Unfortunately, he suffered mental breakdowns and was frequently hospitalised. He also became fixated on proving that the works of Shakespeare were in fact written by Francis Bacon.

admin.multistep-prompt-header: Mode: multistep multiple choice. Match the number of wrong options on each step to the template below. Generate the full chain of steps for every new exercise.
admin.multistep-stem-logic-line: Flow: for follow-up step n, the visible line for the student is the correct answer from the previous step (main correct → step 1, step 1 correct → step 2, …). Options on each step must be plausible next steps from that previous correct result.
admin.multistep-api-field-map: API field names the model must output for each new exercise: main step: exercise, correctAnswer, wrongAnswers (array of wrongs). Follow-up 1: answer_1, wrong_answers_1. Follow-up 2: answer_2, wrong_answers_2. Follow-up 3: answer_3, wrong_answers_3. Follow-up 4: answer_4, wrong_answers_4. Do not use correctAnswer1 or wrongAnswers1 — use answer_1 and wrong_answers_1. After all steps: secondAnswer = final result only if the topic uses it (else empty).
admin.multistep-wrong-counts-line: Template wrong-option counts per step (your new exercises must use the same counts): {detail}
admin.multistep-second-answer-final: Second answer (only if the topic uses it: final result after the last step; leave empty otherwise)
admin.lesson-generated-body: The lesson was generated and saved for this topic. You can review it in Strapi or open it in the app.
admin.lesson-generated-error-body: The lesson could not be generated. Check your connection, admin rights, and OpenAI configuration, then try again.
